sections.body_en:
As a rule, Jews who believe in God and His Torah are trusted regarding the mitzvot, and therefore the Torah commanded that every Jew, man or woman, should fulfill the mitzvot of kashrut himself: slaughter his animals, and make the meat kosher by removing the ḥalavim (forbidden fats), the gid ha-nasheh and the blood, and separate terumot and ma'asrot from his produce, without a kohen or a Torah scholar supervising him. And anyone who is a guest at his fellow's home can rely on him and eat from his food. If he served him meat, he can rely on him that he made it kosher from the blood properly, did not mix meat and milk in his dishes, took care that there were no sheratzim in them, and separated terumot and ma'asrot from his produce. Not only that, but according to the mitzvot of the Torah, even the holy people, the kohanim, rely on every Jew and eat from his slaughtering, for the Torah commanded that every Jew who slaughters an animal for himself should give the kohanim as a gift the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw. This is what the Sages said: “One witness is believed regarding prohibitions,” that is, a person can testify about foods that they are kosher (Rashi, Yevamot 88a, s.v. “ve-amar”; Ḥullin 10b, s.v. “ed”). Likewise we find that every Jewish man relies on his wife that she is careful about the impurity of nidda (Tosafot Gittin 2b, s.v. “ed”). And so the Sages said: “The laws of consecrated property, terumot and ma'asrot – these are the essential bodies of the Torah, and they were entrusted to the amei ha-aretz (unlearned people)” (Shabbat 32a).

However, this basic trustworthiness depends on two conditions. The first is that we are dealing with a person who knows how to fulfill the details of the mitzva. Therefore the custom is to examine a person who has begun to slaughter, whether he knows how to do so properly (Ḥullin 3b; SA YD 1:1; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 119:2). Likewise, when it became clear to the Sages that the amei ha-aretz were not expert in the laws of purity and impurity, they enacted that one should not rely on an am ha-aretz in matters of impurity and purity unless he undertakes before three people to study them and observe them, and then one relies on him, and on his wife and children (Rambam, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav U-moshav 10:1-5).

The second condition is that he does not treat the mitzva lightly; but if he is known to treat the mitzva lightly, one does not rely on him. Therefore, when the Sages in the days of the Second Temple found that, because of the high cost of the tithes, some of the amei ha-aretz did not separate them, they decreed that regarding tithes one relies only on someone who has undertaken before three people to be trustworthy regarding them (Sota 48a; Yerushalmi Sota 9:11; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 9:1; above 8:13).

The basic trustworthiness that every Jew has applies to ordinary situations, such as a person who is a guest at his fellow's home, who can rely on the host to serve him kosher food. But when it comes to merchants, there is a need to supervise them, because of the financial temptation that may cause them to stumble. As the Torah especially warned merchants regarding measures and weights, that they be accurate and that they not cheat with them, as it is stated (Devarim 25:13-15): “You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, a great and a small. You shall not have in your house diverse measures, a great and a small. A perfect and just weight shall you have, a perfect and just measure shall you have, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you.” The Sages learned from the Torah's emphasis, “shall you have” – “that one appoints agardemin (market inspectors) over the measures.” That is, it is a mitzva to appoint inspectors who will examine the merchants and their measures and weights, and punish the cheaters (Bava Batra 89a; Rambam, Hilkhot Geneiva 8:20).

Even a kohen, whose main occupation is in matters of holiness, is not relied upon when a great temptation stands before him. Therefore the Sages ruled that if a blemish of a kind that can be caused by a person appeared in a firstborn animal that was in a kohen's possession, the firstborn is not permitted for slaughter and eating unless the kohen brings a witness who testifies that the blemish occurred by itself. And if there is no witness, the firstborn is not permitted, because we are concerned that perhaps the kohen inflicted a blemish on it in order to permit its meat for eating and to be exempt from the need to tend to it (SA and Rema YD 314:1; above 19:6).

So too regarding sellers of food: since they may profit from selling non-kosher food, there is a need to supervise them. In recent generations, food production has become complex and ramified (above 37:1), to the point that a firm custom has become established not to buy food about which kashrut questions may arise from a factory or a store that has no kashrut certificate, even if the seller observes the mitzvot (see Meshiv Davar 2:7; Igrot Moshe YD 4:1; Naharot Eitan 2:38; Minḥat Asher 1:37).

However, there is no precise definition of the level of supervision required; rather, four fundamental rules guide the level of supervision. The first: the greater the temptation, that is, the more the merchant will profit through cheating, the tighter the supervision must be. The second: the more severe the prohibition that the concern relates to, the tighter the supervision must be. Therefore the tightest supervision is carried out over meat, where a stumbling involves a Torah prohibition and the temptation to cheat is very great, since the price of kosher meat is double the price of non-kosher meat. The third: the more people the merchant supplies food to, the more stringent the supervision of him must be, in order to prevent a stumbling of the many. The fourth: the more complex the food that must be supervised, such as industrial food containing dozens and hundreds of ingredients and food additives, the more professional the supervision must be, in order to cover all the questions that may arise.1

notes_en.en:
The first rule, that where there is financial temptation supervision is needed: the Sages said in Avoda Zara 39b: “One may not buy in Syria – neither wine, nor muryas (fish brine), nor milk, nor Salkundrit salt, nor ḥiltit (asafoetida), nor cheese, except from an expert; and all of them, if he was a guest at the home of a householder – are permitted.” That is, when a person hosts at his table one relies on him, and when he acts as a merchant one does not rely on him, lest he be tempted to cheat and sell non-kosher food in order to profit. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 11:25-26), the Nimmukei Yosef and the Issur Ve-hetter He-arokh, in the Land of Israel, when it was in the hands of Jews and almost all the food was kosher, there was no concern that people would prepare non-kosher food, and therefore one could rely on all Jewish merchants to sell kosher foods. But in Syria and in the rest of the world, since Jews lived among gentiles, there was a concern that they would buy non-kosher food cheaply from gentiles, and therefore they did not rely on an ordinary merchant unless he had a presumption of kashrut. The Rema took their opinion into account, and so wrote the Taz, Ḥokhmat Adam 71:2, and Arukh Ha-shulḥan (119:1-9). On the other hand, according to Rashi, Ra'avad, Ramban, Maharam of Rothenburg, Ra'ah, Ran and others, in Syria there was a special problem with these goods, and therefore there they ruled to be careful about them, but there is no sweeping rule that merchants who earn money require supervision. So is implied by the Tur and SA 119:1, and so wrote the Maharalbaḥ, Shakh and others. Some say that in principle the halakha follows them, but that in practice, whenever there is a concern regarding the food or the merchant, one may buy only from someone who has a presumption of kashrut (Maharashdam, Knesset Ha-gedola). Similarly, we find that since concerns arose that slaughterers would be negligent in checking for tereifot, it was established that Torah scholars would supervise them and check the tereifot (Tur YD 18 in the name of the Rosh; Har Tzvi YD 20; Tzitz Eliezer 9:36; and so above 21, note 6, regarding nikkur [removing forbidden fats and veins]). Likewise we find that with the ramification and expansion of the food trade, in many communities it was established that the local rabbinate must supervise anyone who sells food about which concerns sometimes arise, even if he is known to be God-fearing (Beit Hillel YD 65:5, cited in Be'er Heitev [Tiktin] 65:9 and in Darkei Teshuva 119:7; Sefer Ha-takkanot Be-Yisrael vol. 4 pp. 369-370; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 119:4-6; Sho'el Ve-nish'al vol. 5 YD 81). Since this rule is built on financial temptation, it is consequently understood that the greater the temptation, the tighter the supervision needed.
The second rule is simple, and similarly it is explained below in halakha 7 that to guard against a rabbinic prohibition one seal suffices, while for a Torah prohibition a seal within a seal is needed. The third rule: the more people the merchant sells to, the more he must be supervised (Meshiv Davar 1:30; and see Yerushalmi Demai 2:2). The fourth rule is explained by what we learned in the previous chapter about the food industry, and its essence is in halakha 1.

sections.body_en:
Although it is a mitzva to supervise slaughterers and food sellers, the intention is not that they are not trusted at all; rather, fundamentally one relies on them, but since they may be tempted, one supervises them from time to time. For if we did not rely on them at all, we would need to station inspectors over them at all times, and we could not rely on the inspectors either, and we would need to station inspectors over the inspectors without end. Rather, the basis of everything is the basic trust one has in an ordinary person, which needs reinforcement through supervision when a financial temptation stands before him. Supervision rests on the foundation of deterrence, which is divided into two parts, surprise and punishment:

Surprise: When there is a concern that the business owner or a worker will perform an action that will render the food forbidden, he must know that at any time the mashgiaḥ (kashrut supervisor) can arrive and see him. For this purpose the mashgiaḥ must be given a key, so that he can come to the place at any time without prior coordination and check everything that is done there.

Punishment: If the slaughterer or merchant is caught selling forbidden food, his kashrut must be revoked. As the Sages ruled, a slaughterer who sold non-kosher meat is disqualified forever. And even if he claims that he did so inadvertently, and outwardly displays that he greatly regrets his sin and is doing complete repentance for it, he is no longer relied upon. For since he has lost his credibility, there is a concern that his “repentance” is intended to obtain permission to sell meat, and when he again faces temptation he will stumble and cheat. Only if he moves to another place, and there a rare incident occurs through which it becomes clear with certainty that he has overcome his lust for money, will it be possible to believe him that he has repented (Sanhedrin 25a; Rashba 1:20; SA 119:15).

At the beginning of the period of the Aḥaronim, about four hundred years ago, when the process of professionalization intensified, there were families whose entire livelihood rested on slaughtering meat and selling it, and if the father of the family had been disqualified from selling meat permanently, his livelihood and that of his family members would have been cut off. Therefore the rabbis ruled leniently in his case and arranged repentance for him with fasts and self-mortifications, and after the completion of his repentance they would again rely on him (Maharshal; Taz 119:16; Sho'el U-meshiv, Mahadura Kamma 2:170. See Ḥullin 18a; Da'at Kohen 2).
And in Shemesh U-magen vol. 2 YD 41, on the basis of trustworthiness.

This is the practice today: if it seems to the responsible rabbis that there is a chance that the one caught cheating will change his ways for the better, they punish him by revoking his kashrut for a certain period, arrange a process of repentance for him, and afterwards return his kashrut certificate to him. However, it is self-evident that since general deterrence is weakened by the fact that the revocation of kashrut is not permanent, there is on the other hand a need to increase the weight of supervision over food merchants in general, and especially over one who has already been caught cheating.2

notes_en.en: As a rule, when a person has no incentive to lie, one relies even on a suspect person, as explained in many Rishonim and SA 2:4; 119:7. And even regarding a gentile who has no incentive to replace kosher food with non-kosher, one relies on him that he did not replace it, as explained in Avoda Zara 34b; 39b; SA 114:4; 118:10. And when there is an incentive to cheat, it can be overcome by deterrence. One of the means of deterrence is supervision by a mashgiaḥ who is yotzei ve-nikhnas (“goes in and out”) by surprise, as we learned regarding one who deposits wine with a gentile, in Avoda Zara 61a; SA 129:1; 131:1; above 29:9. Likewise regarding milking by a gentile, in Avoda Zara 39b; SA 115:1; above 30:2. Likewise regarding slaughter by a Kuti – Ḥullin 3a. Likewise regarding a concern of substitution – SA 118:10. Nowadays part of the deterrence and supervision can be carried out by cameras, as cited above 30, note 5. The greater the concern that people will stumble in a prohibition, the more severe the deterrence must be, through more supervision by a mashgiaḥ who “goes in and out,” and more severe punishment for violating instructions. On the other hand, when the concern is slight, one can make do with surprise supervision only once a day, as cited in the Beit Yosef 131:1. Sometimes the supervision and deterrence rest on the public, who may see the violation of kashrut, as cited in Avoda Zara 31b; SA 129:4. When the deterrence is very great, for example when a violation of kashrut would cause an enormous loss, the supervision can be reduced, as cited in Avoda Zara 40b; SA 131:2. Deterrence can also rest on harm to the credibility of a person whose livelihood rests on his credibility, as explained in Menaḥot 43a; SA 114:5. In Igrot Moshe YD 4:1 he elaborated on explaining the methods of supervision.

sections.body_en:
In kashrut systems it is customary to grant two levels of certificates: a regular kashrut certificate, and a mehadrin (enhanced-standard) kashrut certificate. The difference between them lies in two areas. The first: in mehadrin kashrut, when there is no especially great difficulty, one takes into account the opinions of the stringent authorities, even when they are a minority and even when the basis of the law is rabbinic. Whereas in regular kashrut one follows the rules of halakha: when necessary, in a dispute concerning a rabbinic law one rules like the lenient opinion, and in a dispute concerning a Torah prohibition, if there is a clear majority that is lenient, when necessary one relies on it, and if the dispute is evenly balanced, one is stringent. Only regarding the law of lung adhesions in an animal, although this is an evenly balanced dispute concerning a Torah prohibition, does one rule leniently. This is because of the high cost of being stringent, and also because the reasoning of the lenient opinion seems correct, and also because this was the prevalent custom in most Jewish communities. Thus, in this law too one acts according to the rules of halakha in accordance with the tradition of ruling (above 20:8-9).

The second area relates to the degree of supervision. In regular kashrut one acts according to the rules of halakha accepted by most poskim, and one relies on the business owner to comply with the kashrut procedures established with him, and the mashgiaḥ visits the business from time to time in order to check that everything is being conducted as agreed. If he finds that they cheated, he revokes the kashrut, but as long as he has not found a significant problem, one continues to rely on the business owner. In mehadrin kashrut, by contrast, one relies less on the business owner, and generally one requires that there be a mashgiaḥ permanently present who will accompany all the work of food preparation. In addition, even following a slight violation of the instructions the kashrut certificate can be revoked.

As a rule, the Chief Rabbinate and the local rabbinates grant both regular kashrut and mehadrin kashrut, whereas the private kashrut organizations of various kinds generally grant one level of kashrut. The well-known Badatzim (rabbinical courts that grant kashrut) in Israel grant only mehadrin kashrut.

For various reasons, the kashrut system suffers from many problems, chiefly: a) a lack of uniform procedures for defining kosher and mehadrin;
b) a lack of supervision over certain rabbinates and Badatzim, which sometimes do their work negligently; c) often there is a conflict of interest that may cause mashgiḥim or kashrut organizations to turn a blind eye to problems in order to continue receiving payment for granting kashrut; d) competition that sometimes becomes unbridled and is accompanied by defamation that unjustly harms the kashrut reputation of trustworthy people.

Therefore it is proper to act to improve the entire kashrut system: to establish uniform procedures for defining kosher and mehadrin, and procedures that reduce the concern of conflicts of interest, and to require the kashrut organizations to report transparently on their level of supervision, so that the buyer will know what they were particular about and what they were not; and the Chief Rabbinate should supervise all of this reliably.

However, even now, despite all the problems that require correction, overall the kashrut system in Israel is at a good level. There are several reasons for this: first, thanks to the fear of Heaven and sense of mission of the overwhelming majority of those engaged in kashrut work. Second, the fact that most of the food produced and marketed in Israel is kosher greatly helps the preservation of kashrut. Third, the competition between the various kashrut organizations, and the exposure of shortcomings in the media, cause them to criticize themselves and improve.

Therefore, as halakha and in practice, all foods that bear kashrut supervision of the Chief Rabbinate and the local rabbinate, or of a private kashrut organization, are kosher. And generally, foods that bear mehadrin kashrut of the rabbinate or of private kashrut organizations (Badatzim) are kosher le-mehadrin. And if the rabbi or the mashgiaḥ were negligent in their work, and the food a person ate was not kosher, or not of the enhanced standard he sought, the sin rests entirely on the heads of the rabbi and the mashgiaḥ, whereas the buyer who was careful to buy food that bears kashrut supervision is free of sin. And if the rabbi and the mashgiaḥ did their work faithfully and the manufacturer deceived them, the sin rests entirely on the head of the deceitful manufacturer.3

notes_en.en:
The rule that one follows the majority is a central foundation in all the laws of kashrut, as we learned regarding tereifot above 20:4, and as explained below in note 4. And even when one hears of kashrut problems in this or that rabbinate, the majority of rabbinates are always reliable, and even in the very rabbinate in which problems emerged, presumably in most of the places under its supervision the foods are kosher. Therefore, as long as the consumer has not heard otherwise, he may rely on regular kashrut.
Between the rabbinate and serious Badatzim: the problem with the kashrut of many local rabbinates is that the mashgiaḥ receives his wages from the business owner, and there is a concern that he will be deterred from protesting against him. On the other hand, the Badatzim have an incentive to continue granting kashrut, since they earn their livelihood from it, whereas the local rabbi has a fixed salary and has no incentive to continue granting kashrut, and therefore his ruling is free of bias. In addition, the local rabbinate can be overseen by the Chief Rabbinate and by the state legal system, and in this the rabbinate has an advantage (Rav Moshe Bigel in the introduction to his book Ekhol Be-simḥa). However, the fact that the Badatzim deal in enhanced kashrut, in which the supervision is tighter, creates a balance against their conflict of interest, which is reinforced by their fear of criticism from competing kashrut organizations.
Various Badatzim spring up from time to time and grant handsome certificates, but in practice their supervision is deficient. The prudent consumer should try to avoid relying on unrecognized Badatzim, especially regarding restaurants and small factories. Nevertheless, there is no sin on the part of the innocent consumer who does not know that this is an organization of deficient reliability. For if they are known to be negligent, it is the role and responsibility of the Chief Rabbinate and the local rabbinate to protest against them by publicizing this in the religious and Ḥaredi media, and if they do not mend their ways, to demand that they be brought to trial under the Kashrut (Prohibition of Deceit) Law.
There are rabbis who disparage the rabbinate's certifications, and sometimes they are appointed as local rabbis and grant “rabbinate” kashrut without sufficient responsibility, on the pretext that in any case a Jew who is careful about the mitzvot should buy food with a Badatz certification. However, in practice, although their supervision is negligent and deficient, since their kashrut stamp appears on the food, the consumer may rely on them. And if the food he ate is not kosher, the sin is entirely on their heads. One can suggest to someone who is aware of the doubt regarding their reliability that he test them by asking whether they are willing to eat from their own kashrut. If not, it is better that he not rely on them.

sections.body_en:
There is no hekhsher, not even the most enhanced of the enhanced, that meets the requirements of all the stringent individual opinions, for if the hiddur (enhancement) involves high costs, generally even those who are scrupulous are lenient. Beyond this, when it comes to a stringency that the righteous of previous generations did not adopt, since they held that the stringent opinion had been rejected by the overwhelming majority of the poskim, it is not proper for the rabbis of our day to be stringent about it, so that they not appear to be disparaging the honor of the earlier authorities. However, sometimes the righteous of previous generations were lenient about something because the stringency involved great loss or enormous effort, and then, if it is now possible to be scrupulous according to the stringent opinion without great loss and effort, it is proper to be scrupulous about it, because this involves no disparagement of previous generations.

Today, following the ingathering of the exiles, a situation has been created in which the stringencies of one community are not like the stringencies of another, and sometimes a Badatz connected with members of one community customarily adopts the stringencies practiced in that community, and is not concerned about the stringencies practiced in another community. For example, regarding bishulei goyim, there are Badatzim of Ashkenazic immigrants that are not concerned about the opinion of the stringent authorities (above 28:8). Likewise regarding the custom of scalding meat after salting it, Badatzim of Ashkenazic and Sephardic immigrants are not concerned about the opinion of the Rambam and the Ra'ah as followed by Yemenite immigrants (above 22:7). Likewise regarding the stringencies of Ashkenazic immigrants on Pesaḥ, Badatzim of Sephardic immigrants are not concerned about them. Likewise, every Badatz follows the halakhic approach of its rabbis, and sometimes on a particular question they decided definitively in favor of leniency, and they are then no longer concerned about the stringent opinion. It is proper that enhanced supervisions in the Land of Israel take into account and weigh the opinions of all the poskim and the customs of all the communities.

One should also know that there are issues in which the dispute concerns the very question of what the hiddur is, such as the issue of produce in the Shemita year. Many Badatzim are careful not to certify produce grown by Jews under the heter mekhira (the sale permit), and this stringency is so important in their eyes that they prefer to buy fruits and vegetables grown by gentiles, and sometimes even by enemies. On the other hand, as we have learned from our teachers, it is more enhanced in the Shemita year to buy fruits and vegetables grown by Jews under the heter mekhira, since the heter mekhira is a triple doubt concerning a rabbinic prohibition (Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 7:5), whereas buying from Jews rests on two Torah mitzvot: a) settling the Land; b) preferring our brethren over a gentile. Therefore, when we face two options in the Shemita year – regular kashrut based on the heter mekhira, or enhanced kashrut that forbids heter mekhira produce – we should prefer the hiddur of buying Jewish produce over other hiddurim that take rabbinic doubts into account.

Naturally, there are arguments and competition between the various kashrut organizations, and as a rule it is proper for those who are scrupulous to prefer a rabbinate or kashrut organizations that treat their opponents with respect over kashrut organizations that boycott and defame others. And even though there may be no defect in the foods themselves that they supervise, it is proper to keep away from what is ugly and from what resembles it.

These are the main considerations facing those who wish to be scrupulous, and one who does not know how to examine this would do well to consult his rabbi about it.

The division of supervision into “kosher” and “kosher le-mehadrin” exists in food factories and in restaurants, but in practice the ability to supervise large factories is easy compared with the supervision required for restaurants. This is because in mass production, the mashgiaḥ must first conduct a thorough check of all the ingredients from which the food is produced, and afterwards make sure that the factory continues to operate as agreed. In addition, it is easy for a large factory to finance strict supervision, so that in practice even regular kashrut, in terms of the level of supervision, comes close to being considered kosher le-mehadrin.

However, in restaurants that do various kinds of cooking, the work of supervision is more complex, for one must supervise all the types of food that the restaurant buys from merchants who change from time to time. In addition, since the cooking is done by hand by people who are generally not expert in halakha, mishaps sometimes occur. To supervise the restaurant fully, it would be necessary to station a permanent mashgiaḥ at its service, but most restaurants cannot bear the cost involved in maintaining a permanent mashgiaḥ. Therefore, the rabbinate maintains basic supervision that rests on trust in the restaurant owner and the workers to comply with the kashrut procedures established for them, and the mashgiaḥ comes from time to time to check that the established procedures are being kept. In mehadrin supervision, by contrast, the supervision is constant and guarantees kashrut at a higher level.

Therefore, even one who is not accustomed to be careful about mehadrin kashrut would do well to be scrupulous and prefer a restaurant that has mehadrin kashrut, or at least a restaurant that belongs to a kosher chain that is careful about the quality of its products. This applies especially to meat restaurants, since the temptation to cheat with meat products is great, because the price of kosher meat is double the price of non-kosher meat, and over a month this amounts to a very large “profit.” In addition, the prohibitions involving meat are the most severe. However, one who wishes to rely on regular kashrut even in a meat restaurant may do so. And although the risk that he will sometimes eat non-kosher meat is higher, as long as the restaurant has a kashrut certificate, there is supervision that prevents this in the overwhelming majority of cases, and therefore, as halakha, the food it serves has a presumption of kashrut. And if the diner wishes to benefit himself and the other diners, it is proper that he ask to speak with the mashgiaḥ by telephone and verify with him that the food is indeed kosher. Such inquiry improves the level of kashrut, because it spurs the restaurant owner and the mashgiaḥ to comply with the kashrut rules to which they have signed.4

When the kashrut certificate has expired, one should not rely on the restaurant owner who claims that the restaurant is still supervised and that they forgot to bring him the new certificate; rather, one must call a representative of the rabbinate and hear from him that the restaurant is still properly supervised.

In event halls with regular kashrut, when there is a permanent mashgiaḥ present throughout the time the food is prepared and served, the level of supervision is good. But if the mashgiaḥ comes only from time to time, the situation is generally less good, since the temptation to cheat is very great. Therefore, those booking the event should ask to meet with the mashgiaḥ, and only if he attests to them that the food they will receive is kosher should they book the event.

Large and medium-sized hotels are generally under better supervision than restaurants, because the scale of food production in them is larger, and therefore the supervision of them is closer. Nevertheless, it is good for those who are accustomed to be scrupulous to ask to speak with the mashgiaḥ in order to hear that the kashrut procedures are being carried out in proper order.

notes_en.en: The basis for trust in kashrut is that “one witness is believed regarding prohibitions,” and therefore one relies on the mashgiaḥ who attests orally or through the kashrut certificate that the food is kosher. And although the mashgiaḥ receives payment for this, since the rabbis choose trustworthy mashgiḥim and supervise them, one may rely on them. And although people sometimes lie, including people who were considered especially trustworthy, the minority of liars does not cancel the rule that “one witness is believed regarding prohibitions.” Just as, although sometimes two witnesses lie, as long as it has not been proven otherwise, one relies on two witnesses in the most severe laws (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 7:7). And although bad rumors sometimes spread about the kashrut of a certain rabbinate that acts negligently and employs deceitful or negligent mashgiḥim, and sometimes there are stores that sell non-kosher food with a forged kashrut certificate – despite all this, as long as there is no explicit testimony as to exactly where the place that sells non-kosher food is, it is permitted to buy food in all places that have a kashrut certificate from a rabbinate or from a reliable private kashrut organization. First, because of the basic presumption of kashrut of the rabbinate that grants the kashrut stamp, which should not be uprooted without careful investigation. Second, one follows the majority, and most places that have a kashrut certificate are kosher. As explained in Ḥullin 95a and SA 110:3, even if food is found in the street, if in that place most stores are kosher, even though in a minority of stores non-kosher food is sold, the food found in the street is kosher, for one follows the majority. All the more so one may buy in stores that have a kashrut certificate. And one cannot claim that the places where they cheat are considered kavu'a (fixed in place, where the majority rule does not apply), since it is not known where they are, and according to most poskim the law of kavu'a depends on the non-kosher place being known, or at least being such that with slight effort it could be ascertained where it is. And we are not concerned about the stringent opinion in this, since according to most poskim, in any doubt regarding the law of kavu'a one should be lenient (above 2, note 16). However, le-khatḥila it is proper for a person to keep away from doubt, and therefore those who are scrupulous increase supervision, in order to reduce the number of times the seller will cheat and sell them food that is not kosher. By Torah law one follows the majority even regarding meat found in the street, but by rabbinic law, some say that it is forbidden to eat meat that was out of sight unless it bears a sign that it is kosher or it is packaged and sealed with a kashrut stamp (SA 63:1), and some are lenient to follow the majority even with meat (Rema 63:2).

sections.title_en: A Kashrut Stamp on Packaged Food
sections.body_en:
The kashrut stamp on food packages is the testimony that the food in the package is kosher. And although the food is transported from place to place, as long as the package remains closed and sealed as it left the factory, the food in it has a presumption of being kosher. This is the law with all kinds of packaging that are difficult to forge.

Similarly, the Sages established that when food must be sent through a gentile, and there is a concern that he will replace it with food forbidden by Torah law, such as meat, which may be replaced with non-kosher meat, one must seal the vessel or sack containing the food with two seals. And when the concern is of a rabbinic prohibition, such as milk, lest it be replaced with milk of gentiles, it suffices to seal the vessel with one seal. A seal means a special closure that is difficult to forge, such as sticking adhesive tape over the opening of the vessel and signing on the tape in such a way that if the tape is opened it would be difficult to stick new tape there with a similar signature. And if one sticks on another piece of adhesive tape and signs on it, they are considered two seals. Likewise, tying the plastic bag containing the food in a special way that would make it difficult for one who opens it to restore it precisely to its form is considered one seal, and tying two bags – two seals. Likewise, one stamp that is very difficult to forge is considered two seals (Rashba, Beit Yosef 118:9; Igrot Moshe YD 1:56). And likewise a stamp whose forger is liable to punishment by law is considered two seals (Da'at Kohen 229).

Therefore, since it is more difficult to forge original packaging than to forge two seals, all original packaging is considered two seals. True, a professional thief is capable of producing a machine that will forge the packages, but since if he is caught he will be severely punished by law, there is no concern about this. Nevertheless, some are scrupulous to seal with two seals foods regarding which the concern of substitution involves a severe prohibition. Therefore some are scrupulous to seal wine bottles with a cork or metal cap, and over it another plastic wrapping. It is proper to be careful about this with food where the profit from forging its kashrut is great, such as meat in large quantities: in addition to the seal on each package, it is proper also to seal the carton in which the packages are placed. Some are scrupulous to produce special seals that are very difficult to forge (holograms).

When there is no incentive to cheat, as with a restaurant delivery person, one relies on the kosher restaurant that the delivery person is bringing the kosher food that was ordered from it.5

notes_en.en:
It is explained in Avoda Zara 39a-b that one who sends meat, wine, tekhelet or fish through a gentile must seal them with two seals. Whereas one who sends ḥiltit, muryas, bread or cheese can make do with one seal. According to most poskim, the difference stems from the severity of the prohibition of which one is concerned: when the concern is of a Torah prohibition, two seals are required, and with a concern of a rabbinic prohibition, one seal suffices (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 13:10; Rashba, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, SA 118:1). And some say that the difference is between something forbidden in itself, which requires two seals, and something forbidden because of something mixed into it, for which one seal suffices (Ramban, Ra'ah, Ritva, Ran). And some explain that this opinion agrees with the first opinion, for if the concern is of a mixture, it is generally a concern of a rabbinic prohibition, and consequently one seal suffices (Ra'avad, Meiri, the Gra and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 118:3).
According to Rashi, the difference does not depend on the severity of the prohibition; rather, when there is great profit from forgery two seals are required, and when the profit is small, one seal. And although most Rishonim did not write like his interpretation of the Gemara, the basis of his reasoning is agreed upon. So too we have learned that when the gentile has no incentive at all to substitute, there is no concern that he substituted (Avoda Zara 34b; Tosafot Avoda Zara 12a, s.v. “ve-shadi”; SA 118:10; Shakh 1). Likewise, when he is afraid of being caught, because he will be punished for it, one relies even without seals (SA 118:10; see Shakh 129:4; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 118:50). Therefore one relies on a deliverer of prepared food and the like, whenever there is no reasonable concern that he will wish to substitute, all the more so when the situation is such that if he substitutes he will be fired from his job as a deliverer (see Ve-akhalta Ve-savata 5:5). On the other hand, when the concern of forgery is great, one does not rely even on seals, as the Rashba wrote (1:109), in a situation where people were accustomed to forge seals. So wrote the Pri To'ar 119:3. Therefore, with large quantities of meat, care is taken to supervise more closely by means of a shipping certificate, weight and the like, in order to ensure that the shipment is indeed from the kosher place.
The Rishonim raised a difficulty: in Avoda Zara 39a-b it is explained that wine requires the safeguard of a seal within a seal, and so is implied by the words of Rav in Avoda Zara 29b. However, in Avoda Zara 31a it is explained that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, that one seal or a key suffices. According to most Rishonim, the intention is that in addition to the seal, the place must be locked with a key, and consequently this is considered an additional seal (Rambam and Rashba, and Behag and Rif according to most Rishonim), and so it was ruled as the unattributed opinion in the SA 118:1; 130:1. And some learned from Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that if it is known that the Jew will later check whether the food remained sealed with its seal, one seal suffices (Tosafot, Semag, Semak, Terumah, Eshkol, Ran, Ritva). So wrote the SA 118:1 as the opinion of “some say,” who disagree with the unattributed opinion. According to Rabbeinu Tam, a suspect Jew is more likely to cheat because he is less afraid, and therefore when wine is deposited with him two seals are required, and when it is deposited with a gentile one seal suffices (Tosafot there). So wrote the Or Zarua. Some wrote that one may rely on him be-di'avad (Tosafot 31b, s.v. “ha-shole'aḥ”), Roke'aḥ, Issur Ve-hetter He-arokh; Rema 118:1. See further above 29:9, note 11.

sections.title_en: Being a Guest of Someone Who Keeps Kashrut Properly
sections.body_en:
As we have learned (in halakha 1), one who is a guest of someone who keeps kashrut properly must rely on him and eat from his food, for the halakha is that “one witness is believed regarding prohibitions” (Ḥullin 10b, Rashi s.v. “ed”; Yevamot 88a, Rashi s.v. “ve-amar”). And even a guest who is accustomed to be scrupulous and buy food products with enhanced kashrut, when he is a guest of his friend or relative, must rely on the host and eat from his food, because regular kashrut is the halakha according to most poskim and in accordance with the rules of halakha. And although there is merit in the various hiddurim that take the stringent opinions into account, it is more important to increase peace among Israel and to honor the halakha.

However, with firm and clear customs that are practiced by entire communities, and from which the members of those communities are not accustomed to deviate except under the duress of illness, the custom is to be careful about them even when one is a guest. For example, those of Ashkenazic origin do not eat kitniyot (legumes) on Pesaḥ even when they are guests, and this causes no offense, since this is a well-known custom. Similarly, those who are accustomed always to eat only ḥalak (glatt) meat are careful about this even when they are guests. Also among those who are accustomed always to eat only leafy vegetables from special insect-free cultivation, or to soak vegetables in water with soap and rinse them well, there are some who are careful about this even when they are guests. However, in a cooked dish they should not be stringent, because of a sfek sfeika (as explained above 23, notes 7; 21).

And there are many today who are stringent to eat only from enhanced kashrut certifications, to the point that this strictness has become for them a firm custom from which they do not deviate except under the duress of illness and the like. Then, according to their custom, they do not eat at the home of someone who is not careful to purchase all his food products from enhanced kashrut certifications. And although their custom is contrary to halakha, it can be explained that following the crises and upheavals that the Jewish people underwent in recent generations, the tradition of kashrut was damaged for many, to the point that it is harder to know who properly knows the halakha and who is careful to observe it, and in order to avoid doubts and unpleasantness, they took upon themselves rules of stringency of the customs of the mehadrin. In the process they also raise the walls of protection and separation from the public that is less meticulous about mitzvot such as kashrut, or whose positions are invalid in their eyes, and in their opinion this too is a worthy goal.

However, in practice, only with well-known customs of stringency is it proper to be stringent when one is a guest; but with other customs of stringency, as long as the hosts are known to be careful to keep kashrut properly, according to the guidance of the Sages it is forbidden to be stringent, so as not to cause enmity and strife.6

notes_en.en:
This issue is composed of several issues, and we will summarize them briefly. It is explained in Pesaḥim 51b that one who goes from a place where work is not done on Erev Pesaḥ to a place where work is done should not do work. They raised a difficulty: but they said, “A person should not deviate [from local custom] because of strife,” so how may he be stringent when they are lenient? Rava answered that since in any case there are people who have no work, his refraining from work does not appear to be a deviation from their custom. End quote. Thus, if his stringency were noticeable, he would have to deviate from the custom of his place and be lenient like them, for great is peace when the prohibition is not from the Torah (Rosh, Pesaḥim 4:4). Some say that only with a custom may one be lenient, but if according to the stringent opinion it is a full rabbinic prohibition, one should not be lenient (Rabbeinu Tam, Ramban, Shakh 119:20; Pri Ḥadash 19; Mishna Berura 468:23). And some say that even when according to the custom of the stringent it is a rabbinic prohibition, when one goes to a place where the custom follows the lenient opinion, one must be lenient because of strife (Tosafot Pesaḥim 52a, s.v. “mi-makom”; Maharashdam YD 85; Mikra'ei Kodesh p. 199b; Halakhot Ketanot 4; and so they understood the opinion of the Rosh and the Ran). Similarly, the prevalent custom follows the opinion of those who forbid by Torah law the ḥelev attached to the rumen beneath the perisa (membrane), and the people of the Rhineland were lenient about it, and when members of other communities were guests of the people of the Rhineland, they did not eat this ḥelev, but there were some who ate the other foods that were cooked with it. For regarding what was forbidden on the basis of custom, there is no need to be stringent about ta'am ke-ikkar (taste being like the substance itself) in a place whose custom is to permit, because of “lo titgodedu” (do not form factions) (Issur Ve-hetter He-arokh 14:9). Many refrained from eating even what was cooked with this ḥelev, but they were lenient to eat from the vessels in which it was cooked without kashering them (Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Rema 64:9; Knesset Ha-gedola, Shulḥan Gavo'ah and others. And the Pri Ḥadash OḤ 496:24 was stringent not to eat even in their vessels). Similarly, we learned in the Mishna, Demai 4:2, that one may eat for one Shabbat at the home of someone who is not trusted regarding tithes, on the basis of his testimony that he separated tithes properly. The reason is explained in the Yerushalmi there: according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, because of enmity, and according to Rabbi Avun, because of darkhei shalom (the ways of peace). Thus, although this is a rabbinic enactment not to eat from someone who has not undertaken to be careful about tithes, under the conditions of hosting on Shabbat, when it is forbidden to separate tithes, in order to prevent enmity and increase peace, they were lenient to rely on him. Similarly, the Rema wrote (112:15), based on the Maharil, that when one who is careful about bread of gentiles eats with friends who are not careful, he should eat from their bread “because of enmity and quarreling,” for bread is the main part of the meal, and refraining from eating it is very noticeable and may cause enmity (as cited above 28:4). The Rema added: “And one should not learn from here to other prohibitions.” So wrote the Aḥaronim there. From the issues as a whole we learn that the poskim agree that in order to preserve peace and prevent enmity, the guest must forgo customs of stringency (and they disagreed about how he should act in a dispute regarding rabbinic prohibitions, when in the guest's place the halakha was ruled like the stringent opinion: according to Tosafot and those who agree with them he should be lenient, and according to Rabbeinu Tam and those who agree with him he should be stringent). Therefore, one who is a guest of a person who keeps kashrut must eat from his food, for otherwise peace will be impaired and enmity will arise, for we learned in halakha 4 that regular certification is certification according to the rules of halakha.
In addition to this, we have learned that some say that it is proper for the host to tell his guests that the food he is giving them is not kosher according to their custom, but this is not an obligation (Ritva, Yevamot 14b; Pri Ḥadash 119:19). And according to many, it is an obligation to tell them that his food is not kosher according to their custom (Or Zarua, Yam Shel Shlomo Yevamot 1:11; Rema 119:7, Shakh 20, and others). Therefore the Rema wrote (119:7) that a person may eat at the home of his friend who knows his customs, for he certainly will not feed him something “that he treats as forbidden.”
From all this it emerges that when it comes to firm and well-known customs of prohibition, such as kitniyot on Pesaḥ and ḥalak meat, there is no enmity from observing them, and they do not cause a person to be categorically unable to eat what his friend usually eats at home. And regarding these customs of prohibition, according to most poskim the host is obligated to tell his guest that the foods he is serving are forbidden according to his custom, and some say that it is only proper that he say so, but not obligatory. And although we learned that when a person goes to a place where they are lenient, he must forgo his customs of stringency for the sake of peace and preventing strife, and some hold that he must be lenient even regarding laws that are rabbinically forbidden according to his custom, it seems that this applies to a guest who comes to a place where all the local people are accustomed to be lenient, for then the local people may be offended by the guest; but when members of all the communities live together and know the different customs (like Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, who lived in one place), they are not offended by those who are stringent about kitniyot or ḥalak.
But there is no basis for the custom of those who are careful to consume products with a mehadrin certification in their homes to be stringent about this also when they are guests. True, one can explain their custom: following the upheavals that the Jewish people underwent, and the changes in modern lifestyles, the preservation of tradition was damaged, and today it is difficult to know who knows the halakha and who is careful to observe it properly, and as a fence against this they adopted the practice of being careful to consume only mehadrin products. And by not eating at the home of someone who is not meticulous, they resolved most doubts. However, we learned in halakha 4 that the “kosher” certification is the main one according to the rules of halakha, and we also learned in halakha 1 that one must rely on a Jew as long as it is not known that he is ignorant or disparaging. And there is no need to subject him to tests of fear of Heaven and expertise in halakha; rather, every person who is known to observe the mitzvot, and knows the rules of halakha as women knew them from what they saw by their mothers and heard from their fathers, is trusted regarding kashrut. Consequently, their custom is contrary to the guidance of the Sages, and it also involves an affront to the honor of the Torah, in that they treat kosher products as not kosher, and they transgress the halakha that instructed not to be stringent in a situation that may cause offense to the host, enmity and the prevention of peace. There is also a concern that sometimes the position of some of those who refrain from eating kosher food when they are guests has an additional, negative aim, promoted by various elements who wish to separate the Ḥaredi public from the religious public.
And one cannot argue in favor of the stringent that it is desirable to be scrupulous in every issue that is in dispute, as it is stated in Yeḥezkel 4:14: “Neither came there abhorred flesh into my mouth,” and the Sages explained (Ḥullin 44b): “That I did not eat from an animal about which a Sage ruled.” For there the Gemara explained that this is on condition that the permission was based on reasoning, but if it is based on law, one should not be stringent, as the Rema wrote (116:7). And regular kashrut rulings are based on the accepted laws and rules. True, in a matter about which the poskim disagreed, even when the majority opinion is lenient and the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, one who wishes to be stringent with himself may do so (similarly wrote the Arukh Ha-shulḥan 116:25). However, when a person is a guest, according to the guidance of the Sages it is forbidden for him to be stringent.

sections.title_en: Being a Guest of a Traditional Jew
sections.body_en:
One who is a guest of a traditional Jew, that is, a Jew who is accustomed to eat kosher food and is careful to separate utensils, not cooking meat in a dairy utensil and not cooking milk in a meat utensil – if he is known to be a reliable person, one can rely on his word. However, since it is possible that he does not know the halakha properly or is not meticulous in observing it, one cannot rely on a general statement of his that the food is kosher. Therefore, if one wishes to eat from his food, one must first ask about the foods he is serving five questions that cover all the problematic areas. Of course, in order to prevent unnecessary offense, it is proper to ask the questions at the time of the invitation and before the meal.7

The five questions:

a) Regarding meat, one should verify whether it is under reliable kashrut supervision. Those who are accustomed to eat kosher meat can rely on regular kashrut, and those who are accustomed to be scrupulous to eat ḥalak meat should eat on condition that the meat is ḥalak.
b) Regarding fruits and vegetables, one should verify whether they were bought from a store or chain in which terumot and ma'asrot are separated, and if not, one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from them.
c) Regarding vegetables that pose a concern of insects, one should verify whether they were rinsed well. Those who are scrupulous should verify whether they were bought from insect-free cultivation, or were soaked in water with soap and afterwards rinsed. And if they were cooked, even those who are scrupulous may eat them.
d) Immersion of utensils: regarding eating utensils of metal and glass, such as metal cutlery and glass plates and cups, one should verify whether the host immersed them. If not, one should eat with plastic or disposable utensils. In a pressing situation, when there are no such utensils there, one may eat with metal and glass utensils that were not immersed. When this question may cause great insult, one may be lenient because of the doubt (above 31:8).
e) Regarding homemade baked goods, one should verify whether they were in a quantity that is obligated in ḥalla (above 11:6), and if so, whether ḥalla was separated from them, and if necessary, separate a small amount as ḥalla.8

When a Jew brings a cake and says that it is kosher because a traditional person who is careful about kashrut prepared it – as long as the one who brought the cake is a reliable person, one can rely on him. However, one question must be asked: if the dough contained a quantity obligated in ḥalla, was ḥalla separated from it? If there is no certainty about this, one can separate a crumb because of the doubt. If there are fruits in the cake, one must also ask whether terumot and ma'asrot were separated from the fruits. And if it is not clear, one must separate terumot and ma'asrot.9

notes_en.en: We have learned that a person who commits transgressions but is careful always to eat kosher is trusted to testify about the kashrut of his food (SA 119:7). On the other hand, a person who is suspected of sometimes eating non-kosher food is not trusted to testify about the kashrut of his food (ibid. 1). Likewise, one who desecrates Shabbat in public is not trusted to testify about any mitzva (ibid. 7). Seemingly, according to this, one cannot rely on a traditional Jew who sometimes is not careful to eat kosher, and all the more so when he sometimes desecrates Shabbat in public. However, there is a difference between those suspected regarding kashrut and Shabbat desecration in the past and their situation in our day. In the past, when society was traditional, family-based and tribal, it was clear that one who transgressed these mitzvot was frivolous or brazen and scorned the mitzvot, and therefore one could not rely on his word, neither in matters of kashrut nor in monetary matters. However, today there are people who do not observe mitzvot and who are known to be upright and trustworthy (as we learned in Ma'amar Ha-dor by our master Rav Kook, of blessed memory, and as we learned above 29:13 regarding public Shabbat desecrators). So too wrote in practice Devar Ḥevron YD 2:125 and Ekhol Be-simḥa p. 155, that one can rely on the word of an upright and decent person in matters of kashrut even though he does not observe them himself. In addition, when it is easy to obtain kosher foods, one relies even on someone whose reliability is in doubt who says that he bought his foods from a kosher place, in accordance with the rule lo shavik heteira ve-akhil issura (“a person does not leave the permitted and eat the forbidden”) (Ḥullin 4a-b; SA 2:4). On the other hand, one cannot rely on his general testimony that the foods are kosher, since a traditional Jew does not always know the details of the halakha; therefore it is necessary to ask the questions.

The basis for this is that we are dealing with a traditional Jew who is careful about kashrut, who is careful to separate meat and dairy utensils. There is no need to ask whether he cooked with his utensils on Shabbat, in which case, according to the Rashba and those who agree with him, the utensils would require hagala for him: first, because according to the Rosh and those who agree with him they do not require hagala, and also according to the Rashba and those who agree with him, what is cooked in the utensils is forbidden to him but not to others (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 26, note 8). There is no need to ask about non-kosher fish, for a traditional person who is accustomed to eat kosher is careful about this. Nor should one add to the third question whether they also looked at the leafy vegetables after rinsing (above 23:10), for be-di'avad rinsing, which presumably is accompanied by a general glance, suffices. On the other hand, one could seemingly argue that since in practice the great majority of meat in Israel is kosher, and from most fruits and vegetables terumot and ma'asrot are separated, and most people rinse leafy vegetables, there is no need to ask about this. However, as halakha, as long as there is a doubt about it and it can be clarified by asking, one must do so, as we learned regarding the search for ḥametz (Pesaḥim 4a; SA OḤ 437:2). The Pri Ḥadash (437:2) explained that when clarification is very burdensome, such as checking for all the tereifot, one relies on the majority, but when it is not burdensome, such as asking a question, one is obligated to ask. Therefore, in a case where posing the five questions would cause very great insult, for example when the host is an important relative or a very distinguished person, and on the other hand it is not possible to avoid eating there without causing serious strife, one may rely on the traditional host that his food is kosher without asking the five questions. And although most likely he did not immerse metal and glass utensils, in a pressing situation, when asking about this would cause great insult, one may rely on those who permit eating occasionally with unimmersed utensils (above 31:8).

There are no questions about the products from which cakes are made, since in Israel these products are kosher, and only one who makes an effort to look for non-kosher products will find them, and a traditional Jew is not suspected of this. However, one must ask about the separation of ḥalla, and in a fruit cake about terumot and ma'asrot (which are among the five questions). There is no need to ask about sifting the flour, for even if it was bought in the market and was not sifted, be-di'avad the cake is kosher (above 23:15). And regarding the eggs, we have already learned that according to the basic law there is no obligation to check them (above 24:2-3). And there is no concern that the cake was baked in a non-kosher pan, since we are dealing with a traditional Jew who is careful to separate utensils for meat and milk.

sections.title_en: Being a Guest of a Secular Jew, and a Non-Kosher Restaurant
sections.body_en:
One who is a guest of a secular Jew who does not keep kashrut may eat at his home, using disposable utensils, kosher foods from packages that bear a kashrut stamp, or foods prepared in restaurants with recognized kashrut. It is good to ask to know who granted the kashrut to the foods, in order to make sure that it is reliable kashrut. This is, of course, on condition that the host is known to him as a trustworthy person whose word can be relied upon (as explained in note 7).

But one should not eat foods that he cooked in his home, because it is very difficult to check all the problems that may arise. In any case, his pots require kashering by hagala, and the Sages imposed a penalty and forbade foods cooked in pots that require kashering to all those for whose sake the foods were cooked (above 32:3, note 3).

When the host ordered cooked food from a kosher restaurant, one may heat the food in his oven, on condition that the foods remained inside a disposable pan and were wrapped in aluminum foil, in order to prevent vapor from the oven from entering the dishes. And if one heats the foods in a microwave, one must place them inside a kosher utensil, such as a disposable plastic container, and wrap the food together with the container in a bag, in order to prevent vapor from the inside of the microwave from entering the foods.

One may drink coffee and tea at the home of a secular Jew in disposable cups, or in china cups designated for coffee or tea only. In a pressing situation one may use glass utensils even though they were not immersed (above 31:8; 32:5).

One should refrain from entering a non-kosher restaurant, because of ḥillul Hashem (desecration of God's name) and mar'it ayin, and all the more so one should not sit with a friend who is eating non-kosher food there. However, abroad, at a meeting with gentiles, one may be lenient about this, but in Israel, where most restaurants are kosher, one should not enter a non-kosher restaurant even with a gentile.10

Likewise, it is proper not to buy in a store that is open on Shabbat, but when necessary one may buy packaged foods with kashrut certification there.

notes_en.en: At the basis of this halakha is a central consideration of the mitzva of hokhe'aḥ tokhi'aḥ (“you shall surely rebuke”), according to which, out of the mutual responsibility among Jews, a Jew is commanded to protest against his fellow who commits a transgression. True, when the words will not be heeded, it is a mitzva not to say them (Yevamot 65b). But at the very least one must avoid agreeing to his actions by silence, and therefore one should not enter a non-kosher restaurant, and all the more so one should not sit with a friend who is eating non-kosher food there. Similar is the opinion of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv (Ḥashukei Ḥemed, Bava Kamma 83a). But abroad, in a gentile's restaurant where most of the diners are gentiles, there is no such desecration of God's name, and therefore when necessary one may be lenient. Similarly wrote Ekhol Be-simḥa p. 159. And see Igrot Moshe OḤ 2:40; Minḥat Asher 1:67.

sections.title_en: Being a Guest of One's Parents
sections.body_en:
A son or daughter who has become religiously observant, even though their parents do not eat kosher, if the parents are upright people who have kashered the kitchen for their sake and prepare kosher foods for them in kosher utensils, they must rely on their parents and eat at their home (see Igrot Moshe YD 1:54, and above note 7).

A son or daughter who are guests of their religious parents, even if their parents follow the lenient approaches in the laws of kashrut, must eat from their food because of the mitzva of honoring parents. And even if they are accustomed to eat ḥalak meat and the parents are not careful about this, they should eat at their home, for the mitzva of honoring parents is more important than this stringency, even though it is the most important one in the laws of kashrut (above 20, note 11). However, if possible, it is proper to persuade them respectfully to buy ḥalak meat for them. But with regard to hiddurim according to a minority of poskim, it is proper not to ask them to be stringent for their sake.
